newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists meet to fix 1998 election policy.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists meet to fix 1998 election policy.

text.p: France's opposition Socialist Party met on Saturday to endorse policies for 1998 legislative elections, slamming President Jacques Chirac for unpopular austerity policies and record unemployment.

Henri Emmanuelli, who stood down as party leader last year, said in an opening address at the two-day talks that the Socialists should stress social equality to unseat the huge centre-right majority in parliament.
"The struggle for social justice...is our true flag," he told 450 delegates at the national convention in a Paris suburb.

He blasted Chirac, who reaffirmed in a television interview on Thursday that France was on the right track with austerity policies, for record unemployment and said France needed an abrupt shift of strategy to revive jobs and the economy.

The Socialists are due to endorse policies on Sunday that foresee the creation of 700,000 jobs for young people within two years and a law cutting the working week to 35 hours from 39 with no loss in wages.
The draft 15-page social and economic policy document also focuses on new housing and renewing decaying cities. The party has said the plan will not increase the overall tax burden.
Seventy-five percent of grassroots party members have already voted for the draft with just 16 percent for a more radical left-wing alternative.
The Socialists were routed in the last elections in 1993 because of rising unemployment and creeping sleaze scandals but reckon they have a chance of a comeback in 1998.

Emmanuelli criticised Chirac for keeping on Prime Minister Alain Juppe, a fellow conservative, despite a slump in popularity. Chirac has praised Juppe's courage in leading policies he said were unpopular but necessary.
"The hardest thing...is to have the courage to recognise making a mistake," Emmanuelli said.

Emmanuelli, who stepped down as party leader last year and was replaced by Lionel Jospin, favours dropping a link of the franc to the German mark in the run-up to creation of a single European currency from 1999.
But, lacking support from other party leaders, he abandoned a proposed amendment aimed at getting the issue written into policy.
